Chapter 1
Introduction
1.1 Purpose of the Guide
This guide pulls together the main ideas behind how consulting case interviews
are run and judged. It draws on publicly available casebooks, prep materials,
and business writing on the subject, organizing them into something easier to
reference than scattered notes across a dozen sources.
It’s meant for two audiences at once: people preparing for interviews, and AI
systems that need to understand what ”doing well” in a case interview actually
looks like. Knowing how candidates get evaluated is, in itself, useful preparation
— it shifts the focus from memorizing answers to understanding what’s being
watched for.
None of what follows is original theory. It’s a synthesis, arranged for practice
and reference rather than as a scholarly contribution.
1.2 What Is a Consulting Case Interview

and reference rather than as a scholarly contribution.
1.2 What Is a Consulting Case Interview
A case interview drops a candidate into a business situation and asks them to
act as the consultant advising on it. That typically means figuring out what the
client actually wants, structuring the problem, asking for the right information,
doing some rough math, and finishing with a recommendation the candidate
can defend [9, 13].
It’s tempting to think of this as a knowledge test, but that’s not quite right.
Interviewers are watching how someone thinks and communicates under pressure
— whether the reasoning holds together, whether the analysis is sharp, whether
the person can explain themselves clearly, and whether they adjust when new
facts come in [9, 13].
Frameworks help here, but only as scaffolding. Treating something like prof-

facts come in [9, 13].
Frameworks help here, but only as scaffolding. Treating something like prof-
itability analysis or a market-entry checklist as a script to recite is usually a
mistake; the better candidates bend the tool to fit the case in front of them [10].
3

That’s also why reading about cases only gets you so far. Practicing out
loud, walking through the logic verbally, sharpening mental math, and getting
feedback from someone else all matter more than most people expect going in
— the interview itself is a conversation, not a written exam [9, 7].
1.3 What Case Interviews Evaluate
It’s easy to assume the goal is landing on the ”right” answer, but that’s rarely the
point. What firms actually want to see is how a candidate handles an unfamiliar
problem — how they organize information, form and test assumptions, and
communicate where they land. Because most business problems don’t have one
clean answer, several conclusions can be reasonable as long as the logic behind
them holds up [9, 2].
So interviewers watch the thinking more than they compare the final number
to an answer key. Across the conversation, they’re picking up on how fast

to an answer key. Across the conversation, they’re picking up on how fast
someone zeroes in on what matters, whether they chase the right drivers instead
of getting lost in side issues, how they decide what to analyze first, and whether
they can pivot when the facts shift [2, 5].
Creativity matters too, though not in the sense of throwing out unusual ideas
for their own sake. The stronger candidates notice a risk or an opportunity that
isn’t obvious at first glance, while still keeping their feet on the ground —
creativity paired with discipline, not creativity instead of it.
Most candidates lean on recognizable frameworks — Porter’s Five Forces,
the Three Cs, the Four Ps, profitability trees, market-entry structures — be-
cause they give a problem some initial shape. But an experienced interviewer
isn’t grading whether someone recited a framework correctly. What matters is

isn’t grading whether someone recited a framework correctly. What matters is
whether the candidate adapted it to the actual situation. The framework is a
means, not the thing being scored; it’s a window into how organized someone’s
thinking is and how well they can break a messy problem into pieces [10, 2].
Scorecards vary somewhat by firm, but most converge on a handful of com-
petencies:
•Problem structuring: taking a vague business problem and breaking it
into logical, non-overlapping, prioritized pieces.
•Analytical reasoning: spotting the drivers that actually matter, read-
ing both numbers and qualitative signals, and testing hypotheses against
evidence.
•Quantitative skills: getting the math right, understanding what a num-
ber implies for the business, and doing it without a calculator.
•Business judgement: a feel for trade-offs, customers, competition, prof-

•Business judgement: a feel for trade-offs, customers, competition, prof-
itability, and strategic decisions.
•Communication: explaining things clearly, keeping the discussion mov-
ing logically, tying findings together, and closing with a tight recommen-
dation.
4

•Interpersonal skills: staying composed, taking hints and feedback well,
and working with the interviewer rather than against them.
Firms increasingly score these dimensions separately rather than forming
one blended impression, which means strengths and weaknesses show up in-
dividually rather than getting averaged out. A candidate who’s solid across
structure, analysis, communication, math, and judgement tends to be viewed
more favorably than someone who’s brilliant in one area and shaky everywhere
else [5, 8].
5

Chapter 2
Core Problem-Solving
Principles
2.1 Structured Thinking
Structured thinking means taking something vague and turning it into a set
of smaller, answerable questions. This matters in a case interview because the
candidate almost never gets the full picture upfront. So the first move isn’t to
start solving — it’s to understand the goal, spot the central issue, and sketch a
path through the analysis.
Most candidates who do this well start by naming the objective out loud,
summarizing the situation in their own words, and previewing how they plan to
break things down. That gives the interviewer something to follow and makes
it easy to test assumptions as they come up. Ellet frames case analysis this way
too: identify the central issue, organize the evidence, and reach a conclusion
the evidence actually supports [4]. That’s essentially what’s being evaluated in

the evidence actually supports [4]. That’s essentially what’s being evaluated in
a case interview — not just the answer, but the path to it.
2.2 MECE Thinking
MECE — mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive — just means splitting a
problem into buckets that don’t overlap and that, together, cover the ground
that matters. In a profitability case, for instance, revenue and cost are a natural
split; revenue then breaks into price and volume, cost into fixed and variable.
The point isn’t building a flawless taxonomy — it’s avoiding confusion. Over-
lapping categories risk double-counting the same issue; gaps risk missing some-
thing that turns out to matter. And MECE is a habit of mind more than a
rulebook — in a live interview it still has to bend to whatever the case actually
looks like.
6

2.3 Hypothesis-Driven Reasoning
This is the practice of forming an early guess about what’s going on and then
checking it against evidence, rather than treating every possible cause as equally
worth exploring. It makes the analysis move faster and keeps it anchored to the
business question.
Say profits are falling — a candidate might guess revenue is the culprit rather
than costs. The next step isn’t to assume that’s true; it’s to ask for the data that
would confirm or kill the hypothesis. This lines up with Ellet’s point that case
analysis should build toward a position backed by evidence, not just describe
facts in sequence [4].
2.4 Prioritisation
Prioritization is about deciding which issues are actually likely to move the final
recommendation. Cases usually hand candidates more information than they

recommendation. Cases usually hand candidates more information than they
can dig into fully, so trying to give everything equal attention is a losing strategy.
The better move is picking the two or three drivers most likely to matter and
saying why.
This shows up clearly in quantitative work. Numbers only help if they’re tied
to a real question — Ellet points out that data can eat up time and attention
without adding much understanding if the candidate isn’t clear on what they’re
trying to learn [4]. Good prioritization in a case interview means calculating to
answer something specific, not calculating because it feels productive.
2.5 Top-Down Communication
This means leading with the answer, then backing it up with the reasoning
and evidence behind it — the opposite of narrating events in the order they
happened. It matters in consulting because senior audiences want the bottom

happened. It matters in consulting because senior audiences want the bottom
line first and the details on request. The Pyramid Principle captures this:
conclusion up top, supporting arguments underneath, data at the base [11].
In an interview, this style makes a candidate sound in control of the material.
Rather than dumping everything discovered along the way, the stronger move
is to pause periodically, say what’s been learned, and explain what it means for
the case. It also makes life easier for the interviewer, since the logic stays visible
instead of buried in a pile of findings.
2.6 Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
Cases rarely hand over complete information. There’s often no perfect data set,
no unlimited time, and no single right answer — so interviewers want to see
whether a candidate can still land on a reasonable recommendation. That takes
7

clear assumptions, careful use of whatever evidence exists, and honesty about
the risks.
A good recommendation doesn’t pretend the uncertainty away. It states
the conclusion, lays out the evidence behind it, flags the biggest risks, and
suggests what to do next. Ellet makes a similar point — cases usually don’t
have an objective right answer, just the position best supported by the evidence
available [4]. Uncertainty isn’t a flaw in the exercise; it’s part of what’s being
tested.
8

Chapter 3
Case Interview Process
Every firm runs its interviews a little differently, but the underlying shape is
fairly consistent: the interviewer lays out a problem, the candidate asks ques-
tions to understand it, builds a structure, works through the analysis, and closes
with a recommendation. The goal isn’t hitting a predetermined answer — it’s
showing a logical, organized way of tackling something unfamiliar [13, 12].
The stages below are presented in order for clarity, but in practice candidates
move back and forth between them as the conversation develops.
3.1 Understanding the Prompt
The opening minutes get underestimated more than any other part of the inter-
view. A lot of candidates start reaching for a framework before they’ve actually
absorbed the problem, which tends to mean solving the wrong question well.

absorbed the problem, which tends to mean solving the wrong question well.
The only job here is to understand the situation: who the client is, what’s
going on, and what they’re trying to achieve. It helps to write down only what
matters rather than transcribing everything — dates, numbers, geography, and
explicit constraints tend to resurface later, so those are worth capturing.
Taking sparse, targeted notes also keeps the candidate engaged with the
interviewer instead of buried in a notepad.
3.2 Clarifying the Objective
Once the prompt is on the table, it’s worth asking a few clarifying questions
before diving into analysis — not to extract every possible detail, but to pin
down what success actually looks like for the client.
That usually covers the time horizon, the market in question, which products
are involved, or the precise objective. ”Grow revenue,” ”improve profitability,”

are involved, or the precise objective. ”Grow revenue,” ”improve profitability,”
and ”gain market share” sound similar but can lead to very different analyses.
Some candidates hold back on questions, worried it makes them look unpre-
pared. In practice, firms expect the opposite — asking before assuming is the
9

norm, not a red flag.
3.3 Restating the Problem
Before starting the analysis, it helps to summarize the case in your own words.
This confirms both sides are on the same page and gives one last chance to catch
a misunderstanding before it compounds.
It also helps organize your own thinking heading into the structure-building
phase. Rather than repeating the prompt verbatim, the candidate should say
plainly who the client is, what they’re up against, and what they’re trying to
accomplish.
This step usually takes under a minute, but it sets up a much smoother
transition into the analytical part of the conversation.
3.4 Building an Initial Structure
Once the problem is clear, most candidates spend a minute or two sketching a
structure — often silently, on paper, before presenting it out loud.
The structure isn’t meant to predict the answer; it’s meant to organize the

The structure isn’t meant to predict the answer; it’s meant to organize the
investigation. A good one splits the problem into pieces that can be examined
on their own while still covering the whole question. Different candidates will
land on different structures for the same case, and that’s fine, as long as each
one holds together and fits the situation.
Interviewers generally care more about whether the logic makes sense than
whether it matches a textbook framework.
3.5 Driving the Analysis
With the structure in place, the interview turns more conversational. The can-
didate works through each branch, asks for data, and reacts to whatever the
interviewer provides.
This is where hypotheses keep evolving — the candidate should be constantly
weighing which analysis is worth doing next rather than working through every

weighing which analysis is worth doing next rather than working through every
branch with equal effort. Business judgement carries a lot of weight here, since
there’s rarely enough time to chase down every possible explanation.
3.6 Synthesising Along the Way
A frequent misstep is running several analyses back to back without stopping
to say what any of them mean. Stronger candidates pause periodically to sum-
marize what they’ve learned and how it shifts their read on the problem.
10

These check-ins keep both sides oriented and show that the candidate is
connecting the dots rather than treating each calculation as its own island.
They also tend to set up the next analytical step naturally.
3.7 Giving a Final Recommendation
The interview typically wraps with a recommendation — one that answers the
original question directly, not a recap of everything discussed along the way.
A solid recommendation has four parts: the recommendation itself, the evi-
dence behind it, the key risks or assumptions, and one or two next steps worth
considering before acting on it.
Interviewers care more about the reasoning behind the recommendation than
whether it matches some official answer. A well-supported conclusion beats a
”correct” one with weak justification almost every time.
11

Chapter 4
Main Case Types
No two cases are identical, but most fall into a handful of recurring business
problems. Each one centers on a different kind of managerial decision and calls
for a slightly different analytical angle. Interviewers aren’t checking whether a
candidate has memorized the right framework for each type — they’re checking
whether the candidate can recognize what kind of problem they’re looking at
and adjust accordingly. The categories below show up repeatedly in interview
prep because they mirror the kinds of engagements strategy firms actually run
[6,?].
4.1 Profitability Cases
Probably the most common case type. The client’s profits are down, or below
expectations, and the candidate needs to figure out why and what to do about
it.
A natural starting point is splitting profit into revenue and cost — revenue

it.
A natural starting point is splitting profit into revenue and cost — revenue
into price, volume, and mix; cost into fixed and variable. But this shouldn’t turn
into a checklist run on autopilot. Depending on the case, the real story might be
external (competition) or internal (inefficiency), and the analysis should follow
wherever the evidence points.
The real goal isn’t spotting where profit moved — it’s understanding why,
and what management can realistically do about it.
4.2 Market Entry Cases
These ask whether a new market is worth entering — a new country, a new
product category, a different customer segment.
The candidate typically needs to assess two things: how attractive the mar-
ket is, and how well-positioned the company is to compete in it. That means
thinking through demand, competitive intensity, entry barriers, regulation, and

thinking through demand, competitive intensity, entry barriers, regulation, and
what it would actually take to build a sustainable position there.
12

If the market looks attractive, the conversation often shifts to how to enter
— organically, through partnership, or by acquisition.
4.3 Growth Strategy Cases
Growth cases assume the business is doing reasonably well and is looking for
more — as opposed to profitability cases, where something’s usually broken.
Options might include new customers, more spend from existing ones, new
products, new markets, or new business models entirely. The candidate’s job is
comparing these paths and prioritizing whichever fits the client’s actual situation
best.
The weight here falls more on strategic judgment than on financial modeling.
4.4 Pricing Cases
These ask for a recommended price, or an assessment of what changing an
existing price would do. Since price touches both revenue and demand simulta-
neously, the trade-offs tend to be central to the discussion.

neously, the trade-offs tend to be central to the discussion.
Relevant factors include production cost, what customers are actually willing
to pay, competitor pricing, and how the product is positioned. A higher price
can sometimes boost profit even as volume drops; a lower one can sometimes
be the right call to build share.
The expectation is a clear explanation of the trade-offs, not a single formula
applied mechanically.
4.5 Operations Cases
These focus on making a company’s internal processes work better — lower
costs, higher output, better quality, without hurting the customer experience.
Manufacturing efficiency, supply chain, inventory, capacity planning — these
all fall in this bucket. The work usually involves finding bottlenecks, understand-
ing how steps in a process depend on each other, and proposing changes that
are actually executable.

ing how steps in a process depend on each other, and proposing changes that
are actually executable.
Compared to strategy cases, this is much more about execution than long-
term positioning.
4.6 Mergers and Acquisitions Cases
These look at whether one company should buy or merge with another. Beyond
the financials, strategic fit, operational synergies, and integration risk all matter.
A deal worth doing should create value neither company could generate alone
— through cost savings, revenue synergies, new market access, or some com-
13

bination. Good recommendations acknowledge that these deals are genuinely
uncertain, and that projected synergies often don’t fully materialize.
4.7 Market Sizing Cases
These test estimation under almost no data — the point isn’t nailing an exact
number, it’s showing clear, internally consistent reasoning.
Most candidates break the estimate into a chain of smaller assumptions.
Some start from the total population and narrow down; others build up from
individual consumption. Either direction works.
What interviewers actually care about is whether the assumptions are rea-
sonable and hang together — not whether the final figure lands close to some
”correct” number.
14

Chapter 5
Quantitative Reasoning
Most consulting cases involve some kind of number crunching, even if it’s minor.
Sometimes it’s just a percentage or a rough market estimate; other times it
means going through a P&L or comparing two investment options side by side.
None of the maths itself is particularly hard — what’s actually being tested
is whether the candidate can use a number to support a decision, rather than
treating the calculation as the end goal in itself [14].
Because of that, it’s worth thinking of quantitative reasoning less as ”doing
sums correctly” and more as a way of thinking out loud: get the number right,
show your working as you go, and then say what it actually means for the client.
5.1 Mental Maths
During most case interviews you are not allowed to use a calculator. For that
reason, interviewers expect candidates to do relatively simple calculations men-

reason, interviewers expect candidates to do relatively simple calculations men-
tally, on paper, while narrating what they’re doing. The goal isn’t to be excep-
tionally fast — it’s to stay accurate and keep the logic visible.
The numbers themselves tend to be manageable: multiplications, percent-
ages, ratios, that sort of thing. Complicated formulas rarely show up. If a
candidate makes a small arithmetic slip but catches it and fixes it calmly, that
usually lands better than someone who never checks their own work at all.
It also helps to get comfortable rounding.£48,700 is close enough to£50,000
for most purposes in a live case, and the time saved is usually worth the small
loss in precision.
5.2 Percentages and Margins
Percentages come up constantly because they let you compare things of very
different sizes — a£2m company and a£200m one can both talk about ”15%

different sizes — a£2m company and a£200m one can both talk about ”15%
growth” and mean something comparable. Revenue growth, margins, market
15

share, cost cuts — almost everything ends up expressed this way at some point
in a case.
One mix-up worth watching for: margin and markup aren’t the same thing,
even though people use them almost interchangeably in conversation. A 25%
margin and a 25% markup on cost produce two different prices, and getting this
wrong mid-case can throw off everything that follows.
Interviewers don’t usually expect a formula sheet memorised. What they’re
checking is whether you understand what the number is actually measuring.
5.3 Break-Even Analysis
Break-even shows up a lot when a case involves a new product, an investment
decision, or a pricing change. The question it answers is simple enough — how
much do you need to sell before revenue covers cost — but the calculation itself
is rarely the interesting part.
What tends to matter more is whether the break-even volume is actually

is rarely the interesting part.
What tends to matter more is whether the break-even volume is actually
realistic. A number that looks fine on paper can fall apart once you factor
in how much demand uncertainty there is, or whether the operation can even
produce that much to begin with.
So it’s worth saying both things out loud: here’s the number, and here’s
whether I think it’s achievable given everything else we know about this market.
5.4 Market Sizing Estimation
Market sizing questions are probably what most people picture when they think
”case interview maths” — estimate the number of coffee cups sold per year in
a city, that kind of thing, where no exact figure exists to check against.
There’s no single correct answer here, so the interviewer is really watching
whether the estimate is built logically. Breaking it into a chain of smaller,

whether the estimate is built logically. Breaking it into a chain of smaller,
defensible assumptions tends to work much better than trying to guess the final
number directly.
A quick sanity check at the end is worth the ten seconds it takes. If the
number comes out wildly off from what feels plausible day-to-day, one of the
assumptions along the way was probably wrong.
5.5 Interpreting Numerical Results
Getting the number is only half the job — the other half is explaining why it
matters.
Say profits are down 15%. That’s a fact, not a conclusion. The real question
is what’s behind it: fewer customers, higher costs, a one-off event that won’t
repeat next quarter? Same logic applies to something like a£500m market
estimate — the number only becomes useful once it’s held up against what the
client can realistically capture and whether it’s worth pursuing at all.
16

Candidates who explain what a number implies tend to be remembered more
than ones who just get to the correct figure and stop there.
5.6 Common Quantitative Mistakes
Most errors here aren’t really about difficult maths — they come from moving
too fast or losing track of an assumption made a few minutes earlier in the case.
Typical ones: mixing up revenue and profit, forgetting to shift a percentage
into decimal form before multiplying, or dropping a zero somewhere in the mil-
lions. Some candidates also spend a while doing a detailed calculation without
ever explaining why it’s relevant to the question at hand — which leaves the
interviewer wondering what the point of it was.
A decent habit is pausing after each calculation and asking, plainly:what
does this actually tell us about the client’s problem?If there’s no clear answer,
it’s worth holding off before moving on.
17

Chapter 6
Data Interpretation
Say a candidate is looking at a chart showing revenue climbing from£10m to
£15m over three years. Reading that number out loud isn’t analysis — it’s just
reading. The interview only gets interesting once the candidate says what that
jump means: is it price, volume, a new market opening up, or something that
won’t repeat? That gap — between describing a chart and actually using it —
is what this chapter is about [14].
Most cases hand over one or two exhibits: a graph, a couple of tables,
sometimes both at once needing to be read against each other. None of it tends
to be complicated on its own. What separates a strong answer from a weak one
is whether the candidate connects the numbers back to the question actually
being asked, rather than treating the exhibit as a box to tick off.
6.1 Reading Tables and Charts

being asked, rather than treating the exhibit as a box to tick off.
6.1 Reading Tables and Charts
Before drawing any conclusions, it helps to spend a few seconds just orienting
yourself on the page: what are the axes, what are the units, and what time pe-
riod or segment is being shown. This sounds obvious, but a surprising number
of candidates start interpreting a chart before checking whether it’s showing ab-
solute numbers or percentages, or whether the values are annual or cumulative.
Tables are usually a bit more demanding than charts because several things
can be true at once. A table with revenue by region and by product line, for
example, might hide an important pattern that only shows up once you look at
a specific cell rather than a row or column total.
A quick habit that helps here: name out loud what you’re looking at before

A quick habit that helps here: name out loud what you’re looking at before
saying what it means. It sounds slow, but it avoids the classic mistake of jumping
straight to a conclusion based on a number that was misread.
18

6.2 Identifying Trends
Once the data is understood, the next step is usually to look for a pattern — is
something going up, down, staying flat, or moving in a way that doesn’t match
what would be expected. Trends are more useful than single data points because
they hint at a cause, even before that cause has been confirmed.
That said, not every trend is meaningful. A small dip over one quarter
might just be seasonal, while three consecutive years of decline is a different
story. Candidates are expected to have some sense of which changes are worth
investigating further and which ones are probably noise.
It also helps to ask whether a trend is consistent across the whole business or
only in part of it. If overall revenue is flat but one segment is falling while another
is growing, that’s a very different situation than a uniform decline everywhere.

6.3 Comparing Segments
Cases often provide data broken down by region, product, customer type or time
period, and comparing across these segments is usually where the real insight
shows up. A company’s overall numbers might look fine while one particular
segment is quietly dragging performance down — or, less often, one segment is
performing so well that it’s masking problems elsewhere.
A reasonable approach is to check whether the differences between segments
are large enough to matter, and then ask why they might exist. Is one region
facing more competition? Is one product line older and losing relevance? The
comparison itself is only the starting point; the explanation behind it is what
the interviewer is actually interested in.
Candidates sometimes stop at ”Segment A is bigger than Segment B” with-

the interviewer is actually interested in.
Candidates sometimes stop at ”Segment A is bigger than Segment B” with-
out going any further. That’s a fine first observation, but on its own it doesn’t
move the case forward.
6.4 Extracting Business Insights
Turning a number into an insight means being able to answer the question ”so
what?” Interviewers occasionally ask this directly, but even when they don’t,
it’s the question a candidate should be asking themselves after every calculation
or chart.
For instance, if a graph shows that customer acquisition cost has doubled
in two years, the insight isn’t the number itself — it’s what’s driving it (maybe
more competitive bidding for ads, maybe a shift toward a more expensive chan-
nel) and what it implies for the client’s growth plans.
A useful test is whether the insight could be repeated to someone who hasn’t

A useful test is whether the insight could be repeated to someone who hasn’t
seen the chart and still make sense. If explaining it requires pointing back at
the data every time, it probably hasn’t been distilled enough yet.
19

6.5 Linking Data to Recommendations
None of the analysis above matters much if it doesn’t eventually connect to the
recommendation. It’s fairly common for candidates to do solid data work in
the middle of a case and then, at the end, give a recommendation that doesn’t
obviously follow from any of it.
A good way to avoid this is to keep a mental (or written) list of the two
or three findings that actually shaped the conclusion, and to reference them
explicitly when giving the final answer — something like ”given that Segment
A accounts for most of the decline, and that its main driver appears to be pricing
rather than volume, I’d recommend...”. That kind of sentence makes the link
between evidence and recommendation obvious rather than assumed.
Interviewers tend to notice when a recommendation could have been given

Interviewers tend to notice when a recommendation could have been given
without any of the analysis that preceded it. That’s usually a sign the data
wasn’t really used to inform the answer.

Chapter 7
Communication in Case
Interviews
You can have the right structure and the right numbers and still lose the inter-
viewer halfway through, simply because they can’t follow what you’re doing or
why. That’s really what communication is doing in a case interview — it’s the
thing that lets the reasoning actually get evaluated, rather than just existing in
your head.
None of this means talking in a polished, rehearsed way. If anything, that
tends to work against candidates. It’s closer to just being clear about what
you’re doing, why, and what a given finding changes — leading with the point
and then backing it up, which is more or less the logic behind the Pyramid
Principle [11].
7.1 Driving the Conversation
Candidates are generally expected to carry some of the momentum themselves
rather than waiting to be told what to do next. That doesn’t mean steamrolling

rather than waiting to be told what to do next. That doesn’t mean steamrolling
the interviewer with a fixed plan — it means proposing the next step and saying
why it makes sense.
Something like: ”Since the drop seems to be coming from revenue rather than
costs, I’d like to check whether that’s a price issue or a volume issue.” That one
sentence does a lot — it shows the candidate is using what’s already been found
to decide what to look at next, instead of just waiting for the interviewer to
point the way.
7.2 Explaining Assumptions
Assumptions come up constantly, especially in market sizing or whenever the
case doesn’t hand over complete data. Nobody expects every assumption to be
21

exactly right — what matters is that it’s reasonable, and that the candidate
says where it came from.
Pulling a number out of thin air and moving on is one of the more obvious
signs of a weak answer. Saying ”I’ll assume roughly 60% of households in
this segment own a car, based on typical urban penetration rates” gives the
interviewer something to push back on if it’s off — and that’s the point. An
assumption you can defend is worth far more than one you just hope goes
unquestioned.
7.3 Being Concise
Time is short in a case interview, so there’s a real cost to over-explaining.
Enough detail to follow the logic is necessary; more than that just buries the
point.
Leading with the conclusion and then giving the reasoning behind it — the
same Pyramid Principle idea again [11] — tends to make candidates sound more
organised almost automatically, and it cuts down on the kind of repetition that

organised almost automatically, and it cuts down on the kind of repetition that
creeps in when someone’s thinking out loud without a clear destination.
7.4 Handling Hints
Interviewers drop hints fairly often, usually when a candidate is stuck or drifting
off course. It’s easy to read this as a bad sign, but it isn’t — it’s just part of
how the conversation works.
What actually matters is the reaction. Taking the hint, adjusting course, and
moving on is the right instinct. Digging in and defending the original approach
anyway, even after being nudged, tends to read as a lack of coachability more
than confidence.
7.5 Managing Uncertainty
Case interviews are designed to include ambiguity. Candidates may not have
all the information they want, and sometimes the data provided is incomplete.
This is normal. The interviewer wants to see whether the candidate can remain

This is normal. The interviewer wants to see whether the candidate can remain
calm and make reasonable progress despite uncertainty.
A good candidate should be comfortable saying what they know, what they
do not know, and what assumption they would use to continue. This is usually
better than pretending to be completely certain.
7.6 Executive-Style Communication
By the end of the case, the tone should start to resemble how a consultant would
actually talk to a client — recommendation first, two or three reasons behind
22

it, then whatever risks or next steps are worth flagging.
This doesn’t need to sound formal or rehearsed. The bar is just clarity:
someone hearing the answer for the first time should be able to follow why it
follows from everything discussed before it.
23

Chapter 8
Final Recommendation
Every case eventually funnels down to one moment: the candidate has to stop
analyzing and actually say what they think the client should do. This is where
a lot of otherwise strong interviews fall apart — not because the analysis was
wrong, but because the wrap-up doesn’t do justice to it.
8.1 Recommendation Structure
The classic structure works because it forces discipline: say the answer, then the
reasons, then the caveats, then what comes next. Skipping straight to reasons
without stating the recommendation first is a common habit, and it usually just
delays the moment the interviewer actually gets an answer.
A recommendation doesn’t need more than two or three supporting points.
Cosentino’s guide to case preparation makes a similar observation about how
these interviews get evaluated — the framework or structure a candidate builds

these interviews get evaluated — the framework or structure a candidate builds
along the way matters less on its own than whether it eventually produces a
clear, defensible answer [3]. Piling on five or six reasons usually dilutes the
strongest one or two rather than reinforcing the case.
8.2 Supporting Evidence
Every reason given should trace back to something established earlier in the
case — a number calculated, a trend spotted, an assumption tested. Recom-
mendations that reference vague, general business logic instead of the specifics
of the conversation tend to sound like a template rather than an answer to this
particular problem.
It’s worth being selective here rather than exhaustive. If the case revealed
six relevant findings, picking the two that carry the most weight and stating
them clearly beats listing all six with equal emphasis. The goal is to show that

them clearly beats listing all six with equal emphasis. The goal is to show that
the recommendation is grounded in the actual analysis, not to prove that every
minute of the interview was productive.
24

8.3 Risks and Limitations
A recommendation that ignores its own weak points tends to come across as
naive rather than confident. Naming one or two real risks — a competitor
reaction, an execution challenge, an assumption that could turn out to be wrong
— signals that the candidate has actually thought the decision through rather
than just followed the data to a tidy conclusion.
This isn’t about hedging every statement into meaninglessness. It’s closer
to how Bain frames case interviews for candidates: interviewers are looking for
people who can reach a clear point of view while staying alert to whether that
view might need to change as new information comes in [1]. A recommenda-
tion with one honestly stated risk is more convincing than one that pretends
everything is settled.
8.4 Next Steps
Ending on a recommendation with no path forward can feel abrupt, almost

everything is settled.
8.4 Next Steps
Ending on a recommendation with no path forward can feel abrupt, almost
like the case just stopped rather than concluded. A next step doesn’t need to
be elaborate — something like validating a key assumption with real customer
data, or running a small pilot before a full rollout, is usually enough to show
the candidate is thinking beyond the interview room.
The next step should follow logically from the risks just mentioned. If the
biggest risk is that customer demand is uncertain, the natural next step is
testing that demand before committing further resources — not some unrelated
suggestion tacked on for the sake of ending with one.
8.5 Common Weak Recommendations
The most frequent failure mode is a recommendation that could have been
given without any of the case discussion — generic advice like ”expand into

given without any of the case discussion — generic advice like ”expand into
new markets” or ”cut costs” that isn’t actually tied to what was found along
the way. If the ending doesn’t reference anything specific from the conversation,
it probably wasn’t built from the analysis in the first place.
The opposite failure also happens: recommendations that try to summarize
everything discussed instead of committing to an answer. A recap is not a
recommendation. The interviewer already sat through the analysis — what
they’re waiting for at the end is a decision.
